sections.title: What you will build and the path through this course
sections.body:
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes, and the thing you ship with it is a **chart**: a directory of templates plus default values that renders into plain Kubernetes manifests. You already know how to install other people's charts; in this course you write your own. Across seven lessons you build **one real chart called `webapp`** that deploys an NGINX-based web application with a **Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap and HorizontalPodAutoscaler**, and you keep improving it until it is ready to publish.

**Lesson 1 (this one)**: chart anatomy, `helm create`, `Chart.yaml` and designing `values.yaml`.
**Lesson 2**: Go templates: `.Values`, `.Release`, `.Chart`, pipelines, whitespace control, `if`, `with`, `range`, and previewing with `helm template`.
**Lesson 3**: named templates and `_helpers.tpl`: `define`, `include`, standard labels and the fullname helper.
**Lesson 4**: guard rails: `values.schema.json`, `required`, `fail` and `NOTES.txt`.
**Lesson 5**: dependencies: subcharts, `condition`, `alias`, global values and library charts.
**Lesson 6**: hooks, `helm test` and `helm lint`.
**Lesson 7**: packaging, the OCI registry, signing, SemVer and CI testing with chart-testing (`ct`).

Every template in the course is shown together with the manifest it renders to, so you never have to guess what Helm will send to the API server. The prerequisite is `k8s-helm-essentials`: you should be comfortable with `helm install`, `helm upgrade`, releases and `--set`.

sections.title: About this example: Chart.yaml
sections.body: `Chart.yaml` is the identity card of the chart. `apiVersion: v2` means a Helm 3 chart (dependencies live in this file); `version` is the version of the **chart** itself and must be SemVer, while `appVersion` is the version of the **application** it deploys and is free-form. The block shows our file followed by `helm show chart`, the command that prints it back after Helm parses it. Notice `kubeVersion`, which makes Helm refuse to install on clusters older than 1.28.

sections.title: About this example: designing values.yaml
sections.body: `values.yaml` is the public API of your chart: every key in it is something users can change with `--set` or `-f`, so name them carefully and document them with comments. Group related settings under one key (`image.*`, `service.*`, `ingress.*`), give every key a safe default, and use `enabled: false` switches for optional objects such as the Ingress and the HPA. Below is the file for `webapp`, followed by a `helm template` call that overrides one value to prove that user input wins over the default.

sections.code:
# Number of pods. Ignored when autoscaling.enabled is true.
replicaCount: 2

image:
  repository: nginx
  # Empty means "use the chart appVersion".
  tag: ""
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent

nameOverride: ""
fullnameOverride: ""

service:
  type: ClusterIP
  port: 80

ingress:
  enabled: false
  className: nginx
  hosts:
    - host: webapp.example.com
      paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
  tls: []

config:
  logLevel: info
  extra:
    FEATURE_X: "true"
    REGION: us-east-1

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    memory: 256Mi

autoscaling:
  enabled: false
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 6
  targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70

nodeSelector: {}
sections.title: webapp/values.yaml
sections.output:
$ helm template demo webapp --set replicaCount=5 --show-only templates/deployment.yaml | grep -n replicas
14:  replicas: 5

$ helm template demo webapp --set autoscaling.enabled=true --show-only templates/deployment.yaml | grep -c replicas
0
sections.note: Precedence, lowest to highest: the chart `values.yaml`, then parent chart values, then each `-f file` in order, then `--set` flags. An empty `tag: ""` is a deliberate pattern: the template falls back to `appVersion`, so a new app release only needs a `Chart.yaml` bump.

sections.title: Common mistakes when designing values
sections.body: **Deeply nested keys** (`a.b.c.d.e`) are painful to `--set`; keep to two or three levels. **Lists instead of maps** cannot be partially overridden: `--set tolerations[0].key=x` replaces element 0, and a second `-f` file replaces the whole list. **Booleans and numbers as strings**: `--set port=80` is a number but `--set image.tag=1.10` becomes the float `1.1`, so quote tags and use `--set-string`. **No defaults** means `nil` pointer errors the first time a user omits a key. **Putting secrets in values.yaml** commits them to git; reference an existing Secret by name instead.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: A chart is a directory: `Chart.yaml` for identity, `values.yaml` for the configuration API, `templates/` for the manifests, and optional `charts/`, `crds/`, `values.schema.json` and `.helmignore`. `helm create` gives you the conventional skeleton, `version` versions the packaging and `appVersion` versions the app, and good values are grouped, documented, defaulted and switchable. Next, lesson 2 opens `templates/` and teaches the Go template language that turns these values into manifests, starting with the `.Values`, `.Release` and `.Chart` objects.

sections.title: Templates are Go text/template plus the Sprig functions
sections.body:
Every file in `templates/` is a **Go template**: plain text in which anything inside `{{ ... }}` is an *action* that Helm evaluates, and everything else is copied through unchanged. Helm adds the ~70 **Sprig** functions (`default`, `quote`, `upper`, `trunc`...) and a few of its own (`toYaml`, `include`, `required`, `tpl`). The result must be valid YAML, because Helm parses it and sends the objects to Kubernetes.

Inside an action, the single dot `.` is the **current scope**. At the top of a template it holds a root object with the built-in values below; inside `with` and `range` it is rebound to something else, and `$` always points back to the root. This is the most common source of confusion, so keep it in mind.

sections.title: About this example: the first webapp template, a ConfigMap
sections.body: This is `templates/configmap.yaml`, the simplest object in `webapp`. It uses `.Release.Name` and `.Release.Namespace` for metadata, `.Chart.AppVersion` for a data key, and a **pipeline** (`|`) that passes a value through functions left to right: `default "info"` supplies a fallback when `logLevel` is empty, and `quote` wraps the result in double quotes. The `range` loop turns every entry of `config.extra` into one more key. Compare the template with the output of `helm template`, which renders locally without a cluster.

sections.title: templates/configmap.yaml (first version)
sections.output:
$ helm template demo ./webapp -n prod
---
# Source: webapp/templates/configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: demo-webapp
  namespace: prod
data:
  APP_VERSION: "1.27.0"
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  FEATURE_X: "true"
  REGION: "us-east-1"
sections.note: `range $key, $value := map` iterates maps in **alphabetical key order**, so output is deterministic. `{{ $value | quote }}` matters: unquoted `true` or `1234` in a ConfigMap `data` field would be a YAML boolean or number, which the API rejects because data values must be strings.

sections.title: About this example: control flow, toYaml and nindent in one playground
sections.body: This throwaway template (it is not part of `webapp`) exercises the building blocks you will use in every real chart. `if / else if / else` picks a branch by comparing with `eq`; `with` runs its body only when the value is **non-empty** and rebinds `.` to it, so `tolerations: []` produces nothing; `toYaml` converts a values subtree back into YAML text and `nindent N` adds a newline then indents every line by N spaces. Read the `{{-` markers carefully: the dash trims the whitespace and newlines on that side, which is why no blank lines appear in the output.

sections.title: templates/play.yaml
sections.output:
$ helm template t ./play --show-only templates/play.yaml
---
# Source: play/templates/play.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: play
data:
  upper: "WEBAPP"
  missing: "platform"
  truncated: "abcde"
  nodePort: "30080"
  selector: |
    disktype: ssd
  resources: |
    limits:
      memory: 256Mi
    requests:
      cpu: 100m
  indented: |
    disktype: ssd
sections.note: The last key (`indented`) uses `indent 4` on a line that starts at column 0 and shows the difference: `indent` does **not** add a leading newline, while `nindent` does. Prefer `{{- toYaml ... | nindent N }}` at the end of the parent key line; it keeps the template readable and the indentation count obvious.

sections.title: Common mistakes: indentation, scope and nil
sections.body: **Wrong indent count**: Helm renders happily and Kubernetes then rejects the YAML; always run `helm template` and read the result. **Using `.` inside `range` or `with`** to reach `.Values` fails with `nil pointer evaluating interface {}`; use `$.Values` instead. **`default` on booleans**: `default true .Values.enabled` can never return false because false is "empty"; use `hasKey` or `ternary`. **Forgetting `quote`** on strings that look like numbers or booleans. **Leaving `{{ if }}` without `{{- end }}`** produces `unexpected EOF` at render time. Use `helm template --debug` to see the broken YAML next to the error.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: Templates are Go `text/template` with Sprig: actions in `{{ }}`, objects at the root (`.Values`, `.Release`, `.Chart`, `.Capabilities`), pipelines with `|`, flow control with `if`, `with`, `range`, and `{{-` / `-}}` to control whitespace. `toYaml | nindent N` is the standard way to embed a values subtree, `$` escapes the narrowed scope, and `helm template` is your feedback loop. In lesson 3 you will stop repeating names and labels in every file by moving them into named templates in `_helpers.tpl`, then build the real Deployment, Service, Ingress and HPA of `webapp`.

sections.title: Named templates: stop repeating yourself
sections.body:
A **named template** (also called a partial or helper) is a block of template text you define once with `{{ define "name" }} ... {{ end }}` and reuse everywhere. Helm keeps one global namespace for all named templates in the chart **and its subcharts**, so by convention every name is prefixed with the chart name: `webapp.labels`, not `labels`. Put them in `templates/_helpers.tpl`; the leading underscore tells Helm not to render the file as a manifest.

You call a named template with **`include "webapp.labels" .`**. The second argument is the scope handed to the template: pass `.` (the root) so the helper can read `.Release`, `.Chart` and `.Values`. Always prefer `include` over the older `template` action, because `include` returns a string that you can pipe into `nindent`, `quote` or `sha256sum`, while `template` prints directly and cannot be piped.

sections.title: About this example: _helpers.tpl for webapp
sections.body: This is the full `templates/_helpers.tpl`. `webapp.name` is the short name, `webapp.fullname` builds the name used for every object (`<release>-<chart>`, or just the release name when it already contains the chart name, and always at most 63 characters because Kubernetes names are DNS labels), `webapp.chart` feeds the `helm.sh/chart` label, and the two label helpers split **selector labels** (stable) from **common labels** (stable plus informational). Look at how `webapp.labels` itself calls `include "webapp.selectorLabels"`: helpers can nest.

sections.title: templates/_helpers.tpl
sections.output:
$ helm template demo webapp --show-only templates/configmap.yaml
---
# Source: webapp/templates/configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: demo-webapp
  labels:
    helm.sh/chart: webapp-0.1.0
    app.kubernetes.io/name: webapp
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: demo
    app.kubernetes.io/version: "1.27.0"
    app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm
data:
  APP_VERSION: "1.27.0"
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  FEATURE_X: "true"
  REGION: "us-east-1"
sections.note: `{{-` and `-}}` inside `define` matter: without them each helper output would start or end with a newline, giving blank lines and broken indentation wherever it is included.

sections.title: About this example: the Deployment and Service use the helpers
sections.body: Here is the heart of `webapp`: `templates/deployment.yaml`. Every name and label comes from `include`, the replica count is dropped when the HPA is enabled (otherwise Helm and the HPA would fight over `replicas`), the image tag falls back to `appVersion`, resources come from values through `toYaml | nindent`, and the pod annotation `checksum/config` is a hash of the rendered ConfigMap so pods restart when configuration changes. The output below is the real rendering with default values.

sections.title: templates/deployment.yaml
sections.output:
$ helm template demo webapp --show-only templates/deployment.yaml
---
# Source: webapp/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: demo-webapp
  labels:
    helm.sh/chart: webapp-0.1.0
    app.kubernetes.io/name: webapp
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: demo
    app.kubernetes.io/version: "1.27.0"
    app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: webapp
      app.kubernetes.io/instance: demo
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: 9dcb26e9a48ff636239b89def456371eba149ce99f2f513234679f9735959bf1
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: webapp
        app.kubernetes.io/instance: demo
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: webapp
          image: "nginx:1.27.0"
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 80
              protocol: TCP
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: demo-webapp
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
          resources:
            limits:
              memory: 256Mi
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
sections.note: The pod template carries only `selectorLabels`, not the full `webapp.labels`: `matchLabels` is immutable after creation, so it must never contain values that change between releases, such as `helm.sh/chart` or `app.kubernetes.io/version`.

sections.title: About this example: the Ingress and HPA behind switches
sections.body: `templates/ingress.yaml` and `templates/hpa.yaml` are wrapped in `{{- if .Values.<feature>.enabled }}` so they render nothing by default. The Ingress uses nested `range` loops over hosts and paths and writes `include "webapp.fullname" $` with `$` because inside `range` the dot is the current host, not the root. Below, the Ingress template is followed by its rendering with both switches turned on.

sections.title: Common mistakes with named templates
sections.body: **Unprefixed names** such as `define "labels"` collide with a subchart or another chart that defines the same name: the last one loaded silently wins. **Passing the wrong scope**: `include "webapp.labels" .Values` makes `.Chart` and `.Release` nil. **Using `template` and then piping**: `template` cannot be piped, use `include`. **Changing selector labels** in a later release makes `helm upgrade` fail with `field is immutable`, so treat `selectorLabels` as frozen. **Forgetting `$`** inside `range` or `with` when calling a helper that needs the root.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: `define` creates a chart-wide named template, `include name .` renders it to a pipeable string, and `_helpers.tpl` is where they live, always prefixed with the chart name. `webapp` now has a fullname helper, split selector and common labels, and Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Ingress and HPA templates that all use them. The chart works, but it will happily accept `replicaCount: lots`. Lesson 4 adds guard rails: a JSON Schema for values, `required` and `fail` for custom errors, and a `NOTES.txt` that tells the user what to do next.

lessons.title: Validate values: schema, required, fail and NOTES.txt
lessons.summary: Add guard rails to webapp with a JSON Schema, custom required/fail errors and a helpful NOTES.txt.
objectives: Write a values.schema.json with types, ranges, enums and required keys
Use required and fail for cross-field rules with clear messages
Preview NOTES.txt with a client-side dry run
Avoid over-strict schemas that break parent charts

sections.title: Three layers of guard rails
sections.body:
A chart that accepts anything fails late and confusingly: a typo such as `image.pullpolicy` is silently ignored, `replicaCount: lots` renders a manifest the API server rejects with a cryptic message, and a forgotten database host becomes a crash loop. Helm gives you three layers of defence, from cheapest to most flexible:

**1. `values.schema.json`**: a JSON Schema that Helm checks on every `install`, `upgrade`, `template` and `lint`, before any template is rendered. Use it for types, ranges, enums and required keys.
**2. `required` and `fail`** inside templates: custom, readable errors for rules a schema cannot express, such as "if the Ingress is enabled there must be at least one host".
**3. `NOTES.txt`**: not validation, but the last guard rail for humans: it tells the user what was deployed and the exact next command to run.

sections.title: About this example: values.schema.json and the errors it produces
sections.body: This schema sits next to `values.yaml`. `required` at the top makes `image` and `service` mandatory, `minimum`/`maximum` bound numbers, `enum` restricts strings to a closed set, and `additionalProperties: false` on `image` turns typos into errors (we deliberately do **not** set it at the top level, because parent charts inject extra keys such as `global`). The four commands below break one rule each; read the JSON pointer (`/replicaCount`) to find the offending key.

sections.title: values.schema.json
sections.output:
$ helm template demo webapp --set replicaCount=0
Error: values don't meet the specifications of the schema(s) in the following chart(s):
webapp:
- at '/replicaCount': minimum: got 0, want 1

$ helm template demo webapp --set service.type=Nodeport
Error: values don't meet the specifications of the schema(s) in the following chart(s):
webapp:
- at '/service/type': value must be one of 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', 'LoadBalancer'

$ helm template demo webapp --set image.pullpolicy=Always
Error: values don't meet the specifications of the schema(s) in the following chart(s):
webapp:
- at '/image': additional properties 'pullpolicy' not allowed

$ helm template demo webapp --set replicaCount=lots
Error: values don't meet the specifications of the schema(s) in the following chart(s):
webapp:
- at '/replicaCount': got string, want integer
sections.note: The exact wording of schema errors depends on the Helm release (Helm 3 prints messages like `Must be greater than or equal to 1`; Helm 4 uses the JSON-pointer form shown here), but all of them name the chart and the key. Use JSON Schema draft-07 or later features sparingly; `helm lint` and `helm install` fail the same way, so CI catches bad values too.

sections.title: About this example: required and fail in a template
sections.body: `required "message" value` stops rendering with your message when the value is empty or missing, and returns the value otherwise, so you can assign it to a variable in one step. `fail "message"` stops unconditionally and is meant for `if` blocks that check combinations of values. The scratch template below uses both; the three commands show the failing and the passing paths. Notice the `{{- ... -}}` on every line: the file must render nothing before `apiVersion`.

$ helm template g ./guard

Use --debug flag to render out invalid YAML

$ helm template g ./guard --set db.host=pg.prod.svc
---
# Source: guard/templates/config.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: guard
data:

$ helm template g ./guard --set db.host=pg.prod.svc --set ingress.enabled=true
Error: execution error at (guard/templates/config.yaml:3:4): ingress.enabled=true needs at least one entry in ingress.hosts

Use --debug flag to render out invalid YAML
sections.note: Write error messages that tell the user **how to fix** the problem (`set it with --set db.host=...`). Prefer the schema for simple rules and keep `fail` for cross-field rules. Remember `required` treats an empty string as missing, which is usually what you want for hostnames and secrets names.

sections.title: About this example: NOTES.txt
sections.body: `templates/NOTES.txt` is rendered like any template but printed to the terminal after `helm install` and `helm upgrade` (and again by `helm get notes`). It can use `.Values`, `include` and conditionals, so it can show the right access instructions for the chosen Service type or Ingress. Because `helm template` does not print it, preview it with a client-side dry run, as in the command below, which cuts the output down to the notes section.

sections.title: templates/NOTES.txt
sections.output:
$ helm install demo webapp -n prod --dry-run=client | sed -n '/^NOTES:/,$p'
NOTES:
demo-webapp 1.27.0 is deployed in namespace prod.

Reach it from your laptop with a port-forward:
  kubectl --namespace prod port-forward svc/demo-webapp 8080:80
  curl http://127.0.0.1:8080

Check the rollout:
  kubectl --namespace prod rollout status deploy/demo-webapp

$ helm install demo webapp -n prod --dry-run=client --set ingress.enabled=true | sed -n '/^NOTES:/,$p'
NOTES:
demo-webapp 1.27.0 is deployed in namespace prod.

Open the application:
  http://webapp.example.com/

Check the rollout:
  kubectl --namespace prod rollout status deploy/demo-webapp
sections.note: `--dry-run=client` renders locally without contacting the cluster (in Helm 3 plain `--dry-run` behaves the same; `--dry-run=server` also validates against the API server and runs admission webhooks). Use `--create-namespace -n prod` on a real install.

sections.title: Common mistakes with validation
sections.body: **Schema too strict at the top level**: `additionalProperties: false` on the root rejects `global` and subchart values (lesson 5); only use it on objects you own. **Schema and values drift**: add every new key to the schema in the same commit. **Using `fail` where the schema would do**: the schema reports all violations at once, `fail` reports one at a time. **Secrets in error messages**: never print `.Values.password` in a `fail` or `required` message. **NOTES.txt that errors**: a nil value in the notes fails the whole install after resources were created, so test it with `--dry-run`.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: `values.schema.json` validates types, ranges, enums and required keys before rendering; `required` and `fail` give precise custom errors for rules the schema cannot express; `NOTES.txt` ends an install with the exact next steps. `webapp` now rejects `replicaCount=0`, a misspelt `Nodeport` and an unknown `image.pullpolicy`. Lesson 5 extends the chart with other charts: you will add a subchart dependency (Redis for caching), switch it with `condition`, run it twice with `alias`, share values with `global`, and learn what a library chart is.

lessons.title: Dependencies, subcharts and library charts
lessons.summary: Add a subchart to webapp, control it with condition, alias and global values, and share helpers with a library chart.
objectives: Declare dependencies in Chart.yaml and fetch them with helm dependency update
Explain Chart.lock and helm dependency build
Pass values to subcharts and share global values
Switch subcharts with condition and include copies with alias
Build and use a library chart

sections.title: Why dependencies, and how a chart finds them
sections.body:
Real applications need a database, a cache or a metrics exporter. Instead of copying their manifests into your chart, you declare them as **dependencies** in `Chart.yaml`. A dependency is another chart (a **subchart**) that Helm renders together with the parent as part of the same release. Where the chart is fetched from is the `repository` field: an HTTP chart repository (`https://charts.example.com`), an **OCI registry** (`oci://registry.example.com/charts`), or a local path (`file://../cache`), which is perfect while developing two charts side by side.

`helm dependency update` downloads each dependency into `charts/` as a `.tgz` and writes **`Chart.lock`**, which pins the exact resolved versions and a digest; `helm dependency build` reinstalls strictly from the lock file, which is what CI should use. Subcharts are namespaced by their name for values, and one chart cannot see the other's values unless they are `global`. In this lesson we add a Redis-like `cache` subchart and a **library chart** to `webapp`.

sections.title: About this example: declaring and fetching dependencies
sections.body: The block shows the `dependencies:` list appended to `webapp/Chart.yaml`, then the commands that fetch and list them, and the generated `Chart.lock`. `cache` has a `condition`, a values path that decides at render time whether the subchart is included at all. `platform-lib` is a library chart (below) and needs none. Look at the `charts/` listing: the packaged subcharts are now part of the chart, so you commit `Chart.lock` and usually git-ignore `charts/*.tgz`.

sections.code:
dependencies:
  - name: cache
    version: 0.1.0
    repository: file://../cache
    condition: cache.enabled
  - name: platform-lib
    version: 1.0.0
    repository: file://../platform-lib

sections.output:
$ helm dependency update webapp
Saving 2 charts
Deleting outdated charts

$ ls webapp/charts
cache-0.1.0.tgz  platform-lib-1.0.0.tgz

$ helm dependency list webapp
NAME        	VERSION	REPOSITORY            	STATUS
cache       	0.1.0  	file://../cache       	ok    
platform-lib	1.0.0  	file://../platform-lib	ok    

$ cat webapp/Chart.lock

- name: cache
  repository: file://../cache
  version: 0.1.0
- name: platform-lib
  repository: file://../platform-lib
  version: 1.0.0
digest: sha256:8793ceb173dd30609711d745991d94b83d19d3ff32c15a7cc96b650f057a4b18

Run `helm dependency update` again whenever you change the `dependencies` list.

Meaning

sections.title: About this example: values flow, condition and global
sections.body: Values for a subchart live under a key with the subchart's name: `cache.replicaCount: 2` in the parent overrides the `replicaCount` default in `cache/values.yaml`. Anything under **`global:`** is visible to the parent **and every subchart** as `.Values.global.*`, which is how you share things like environment names or image registries. The `cache.enabled` boolean is the `condition`. The commands render the whole release, then switch the subchart off, and finally print the subchart Deployment to prove both overrides arrived.

sections.code:
# Passed to the "cache" subchart: keys under the subchart name.
cache:
  enabled: true
  replicaCount: 2

# Visible to the parent and to every subchart as .Values.global.*
global:
  environment: staging
  system: shop

owner: team-web

With `cache.enabled=false` no file from `charts/cache` appears. In the subchart, `global.environment` arrives as `"staging"`. A subchart cannot read its parent's non-global values, which keeps it reusable.

sections.title: About this example: aliases and a library chart
sections.body: An **alias** lets you include the same subchart more than once with separate values: the parent below pulls `cache` twice as `sessions` and `pages`, each configured under its own key. A **library chart** (`type: library` in `Chart.yaml`) contains only named templates and renders no manifests of its own; you depend on it and `include` its helpers, so every chart in the company shares the same labels. The first block is the library template, the second the scratch `stack` chart with aliases and the rendered result.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v2
name: platform-lib
description: Shared helpers for all company charts
type: library
version: 1.0.0

# templates/_labels.tpl
{{- define "platform-lib.labels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/part-of: {{ .Values.global.system | default "platform" }}
company.example.com/owner: {{ .Values.owner | default "unassigned" | quote }}
{{- end -}}

# webapp/templates/lib-demo.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: {{ include "webapp.fullname" . }}-labels-demo
  labels:
    {{- include "platform-lib.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
data: {}

# stack/Chart.yaml dependencies
dependencies:
  - name: cache
    alias: sessions
    version: 0.1.0
    repository: file://../cache
  - name: cache
    alias: pages
    version: 0.1.0
    repository: file://../cache
# stack/values.yaml
sessions:
  replicaCount: 1
pages:
  replicaCount: 3
  image:
    tag: 7.4-alpine

sections.note: Library charts cannot be installed (`helm install` on one fails) and are ideal for the helpers from lesson 3. Inside an included library template the dot is the **caller's** scope, so `.Chart.Name` is `webapp` and `.Values.owner` comes from the parent. Prefix library template names with the library name (`platform-lib.labels`) to avoid collisions.

sections.title: Common mistakes with dependencies
sections.body: **Forgetting `helm dependency update`** gives `found in Chart.yaml, but missing in charts/ directory`. **Subchart values at the wrong level**: `replicaCount: 2` at the top changes the parent, not the cache; it must be under `cache:`. **Expecting a subchart to read parent values**: only `global` crosses the boundary. **Unpinned versions** such as `*` make builds irreproducible: commit `Chart.lock` and use `helm dependency build` in CI. **Name collisions**: two subcharts defining the same named template; always prefix. **Dashes in aliases** are awkward in `--set`; prefer `sessions` to `session-cache`.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: Dependencies live in `Chart.yaml`, are fetched into `charts/` by `helm dependency update` and pinned by `Chart.lock`. Subchart values go under the subchart name (or alias), `global` values are shared, `condition` and `tags` switch subcharts on and off, `alias` allows several copies, and library charts distribute reusable named templates. In lesson 6 we add behaviour around the release itself: hooks that run a Job before an upgrade, test pods run by `helm test`, and `helm lint` to catch problems before they ship.

lessons.title: Hooks, helm test and helm lint
lessons.summary: Run migrations before upgrades, verify releases with test hooks and catch mistakes with lint.
objectives: Explain hook events, weights and delete policies
Write a pre-upgrade migration Job hook
Write a test hook and run it with helm test
Use helm lint and its --strict flag in a workflow
Avoid hook pitfalls that block releases

sections.title: What a hook is and when it runs
sections.body:
A **hook** is an ordinary Kubernetes resource (usually a Job or Pod) in `templates/` that carries the annotation `helm.sh/hook`. Helm does not treat it as part of the release's normal resources: it creates it at a specific moment of the release lifecycle, **waits for it to finish** (a Job to complete, a Pod to succeed), and only then continues. If a hook fails, the whole `install` or `upgrade` fails. Typical uses are database migrations before an upgrade, a smoke test after it, or cleanup before delete.

Two more annotations shape hook behaviour. **`helm.sh/hook-weight`** is a string number; hooks of the same event run in ascending weight order (ties break by resource kind, then name). **`helm.sh/hook-delete-policy`** says when Helm deletes the hook object: `before-hook-creation` (default, deletes the previous one before creating a new one), `hook-succeeded`, or `hook-failed`. Because hooks are not tracked as release resources, `helm uninstall` will not remove leftovers unless a delete policy does.

sections.title: Hook events
head: Annotation value
Runs
Typical use
Note
rows: After templates render, before any resource is created
create a database or run a first-time setup
After all resources are created and ready
release is already deployed if this fails

export data, deregister from a service

Only when you run helm test

sections.title: About this example: a migration Job as pre-install and pre-upgrade hook
sections.body: This is `templates/job-migrate.yaml` in the hooks version of `webapp`. The three annotations make it run **before** every install and upgrade (`pre-install,pre-upgrade`), at weight `-5` so it runs ahead of any other pre-hooks with higher weights, and be removed when it succeeds or when a new run starts. `activeDeadlineSeconds` and `backoffLimit` stop a stuck migration from blocking the release forever. The output of `helm template` shows the object with its annotations, and `--no-hooks` proves hooks are a separate class of resource.

sections.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ include "webapp.fullname" . }}-migrate
  labels:
    {{- include "webapp.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-install,pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
spec:
  backoffLimit: 1
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 300
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        {{- include "webapp.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }}
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo running migrations for {{ .Release.Name }} && sleep 3"]

sections.title: About this example: a test hook and the install, upgrade, test flow
sections.body: `templates/tests/test-connection.yaml` is a Pod with `helm.sh/hook: test`. It calls the chart's Service with `wget` and exits 0 on success, so it validates DNS, the Service selector and the application together. It only runs when you execute **`helm test <release>`** after an install. The block shows the Pod and then a typical session on a real cluster: the pre-upgrade Job runs first, the release becomes `deployed`, and the test passes.

    "helm.sh/hook": test
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: wget
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["wget"]
      args: ["-qO-", "http://{{ include "webapp.fullname" . }}:{{ .Values.service.port }}"]

sections.title: About this example: helm lint finds problems before the cluster does
sections.body: `helm lint` runs static checks on the chart: Chart.yaml rules, template rendering, YAML validity and the values schema. The first run below is the clean chart. The second uses a copy of the chart where `version` was changed to `"1.0"` and one line of `deployment.yaml` lost two spaces of indentation; lint reports a SemVer warning and a YAML parse error, and exits non-zero so CI fails. `--strict` turns warnings into errors and `--set` or `-f` lint with specific values.

sections.title: Common mistakes with hooks and tests
sections.body: **Hooks that never finish**: a Job without `activeDeadlineSeconds` hangs the release until `--timeout` (default 5 minutes). **Non-idempotent migrations** that break on the second run. **Hook resources left behind** because no delete policy was set: the next install fails with `already exists`. **Hook needs resources that do not exist yet**: a `pre-install` hook cannot use a ConfigMap or Secret of the same chart unless that resource is itself a pre-install hook with a lower weight. **Treating `helm test` as a unit test**: it needs a live release and checks the deployment, not the templates. **Forgetting `--wait`** so tests run before pods are ready.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: Hooks are annotated resources that Helm runs at lifecycle events and waits for; weights order them and delete policies clean them up. `helm test` runs Pods annotated `test` against a live release, and `helm lint` (plus `helm template` and `--dry-run=server`) catches mistakes without touching production. `webapp` now has a migration hook and a connection test. In the final lesson you package the chart, publish it to an OCI registry, sign it, version it with SemVer and wire lint, template and install tests into CI with chart-testing.

lessons.title: Package, publish, version and test in CI
lessons.summary: Package webapp, publish it to an HTTP repository or OCI registry, sign it, version it with SemVer and test it in CI with chart-testing.
objectives: Package a chart and build a repository index.yaml
Push and install charts through an OCI registry
Sign a chart and verify provenance
Apply SemVer to version and appVersion correctly
Configure ct lint and ct install in a CI pipeline

sections.title: From a directory to something other people can install
sections.body:
A chart directory is for authors. To share it, you **package** it into a versioned archive (`webapp-0.2.0.tgz`) and put that archive somewhere installers can reach: a classic **HTTP chart repository** (a static web server holding the `.tgz` files plus an `index.yaml` catalogue) or, increasingly the default, an **OCI registry** such as Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR or Harbor, where a chart is stored just like a container image. Installers then run `helm repo add` + `helm install repo/webapp`, or `helm install oci://...` directly.

Two version numbers travel with the package. **`version`** is the chart's own SemVer and must change on every published change, because registries treat a version as immutable. **`appVersion`** is informational: the version of the application the chart deploys (here the NGINX tag). Bump the chart's **patch** for fixes in templates, **minor** for backward-compatible new values or objects, and **major** when an upgrade requires users to change their values or when you remove or rename a value.

sections.title: SemVer for charts: which part to bump
head: Change in the chart
Bump
Example
Why
rows: Fix a label typo or template bug, no new values
Add an optional value such as autoscaling.behavior
new keys have defaults, old values still work
Rename or remove a value, change a selector, raise minimum Kubernetes
users must edit values or recreate objects
the packaging changed even if templates did not
sorts before 0.3.0 and is skipped unless --devel is used
SemVer allows breaking changes in minor versions, so say so in the README

sections.title: About this example: helm package and an HTTP repository index
sections.body: `helm package` validates the chart, archives it as `<name>-<version>.tgz` and can override versions on the command line, which is handy in CI (`--version 0.2.0 --app-version 1.27.1`). `helm repo index` scans a directory of archives and writes `index.yaml` with name, version, digest and download URL of each chart; upload both to any static host (S3 behind CloudFront, GitHub Pages, nginx) and you have a repository. Check the `digest` and `urls` fields in the index: they are what `helm install` downloads and verifies.

helm package webapp --version 0.2.0 --app-version 1.27.1 -d out
ls -l out
helm repo index out --url https://charts.example.com
cat out/index.yaml

sections.title: About this example: publishing to an OCI registry and signing
sections.body: With OCI there is no `index.yaml` to maintain: `helm push` uploads the archive as an artifact whose tag is the chart version, and `helm pull` or `helm install oci://...` fetches it. You authenticate with `helm registry login`. **Signing** adds provenance: `helm package --sign` creates a `.prov` file containing the chart hash signed with your PGP key, and `helm verify` (or `--verify` on install/pull) checks it against the public key. Sigstore/cosign signing of the OCI artifact is a common modern alternative. The session below uses a fictional ECR registry and shows the shape of the output.

helm install demo oci://123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/charts/webapp --version 0.2.0 -n prod --create-namespace
helm package webapp --sign --key 'Platform Team' --keyring ~/.gnupg/secring.gpg -d out
helm verify out/webapp-0.1.0.tgz --keyring ~/.gnupg/pubring.gpg

sections.title: About this example: testing charts in CI with chart-testing (ct)
sections.body: **chart-testing (`ct`)** is the Helm project's tool for CI. `ct lint` runs `helm lint`, validates `Chart.yaml` and YAML style, and enforces that the chart `version` was bumped compared with the target branch (`check-version-increment`). `ct install` creates a throwaway namespace on a kind cluster, installs every changed chart once per file in its `ci/*-values.yaml`, and runs `helm test`. The first block is `ct.yaml`, the second a CI-only values file that turns on Ingress and HPA so those templates are exercised, the third a GitHub Actions workflow, and the output is a lint run.

sections.code:
# ct.yaml
remote: origin
target-branch: main
chart-dirs:
  - charts
check-version-increment: true
validate-maintainers: false
helm-extra-args: --timeout 300s

# charts/webapp/ci/ingress-hpa-values.yaml
ingress:
  enabled: true
autoscaling:
  enabled: true

# .github/workflows/chart-ci.yaml
name: chart-ci
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["charts/**"]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: azure/setup-helm@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - uses: helm/chart-testing-action@v2.6.1
      - name: Lint
        run: ct lint --config ct.yaml
      - uses: helm/kind-action@v1.10.0
      - name: Install and test on kind
        run: ct install --config ct.yaml

sections.note: With `check-version-increment: true` a pull request that changes templates but not `version` fails, which keeps published versions immutable. A typical release job on the main branch then runs `helm package`, `helm push` and, if you also host an HTTP repository, `helm repo index --merge`. Pin action versions to a commit SHA in security-sensitive pipelines.

sections.title: Common mistakes when publishing
sections.body: **Re-publishing the same version** with different content: caches and GitOps tools (Argo CD, Flux) keep the old archive, so bump `version` every time. **Using `appVersion` as the only version**: it is not used for resolution. **Forgetting `helm dependency build`** before `helm package`, which ships a chart with missing subcharts. **Using `latest`-style ranges** in consumer charts. **Putting secrets or `.git` in the archive**: check `.helmignore` and `tar tzf webapp-0.2.0.tgz`. **Pushing without `ci/` values coverage**, so optional templates (Ingress, HPA) are never rendered by the pipeline. **Signing key lost**: store the private key and passphrase in your CI secret manager and document the public key for consumers.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: You packaged `webapp` with `helm package`, indexed it for an HTTP repository or pushed it to an OCI registry, signed it for provenance, versioned it by SemVer rules (chart `version` versus `appVersion`), and wired `ct lint` and `ct install` into CI so every change is linted, version-checked, installed on kind and tested. Together with the earlier lessons you now own the full chart lifecycle: scaffold, template, factor into helpers, validate, compose with subcharts, hook into releases, test and ship. To deploy such charts continuously with a reconciler instead of `helm install` by hand, continue with the GitOps lesson in the delivery course.
